title: Contribution of copy number variants to schizophrenia in East Asian populations.
data_url: https://zenodo.org/records/19058548 (analysis code, CC-BY-4.0); supplementary tables at https://static-content.springer.com/esm/art%3A10.1038%2Fs41588-026-02732-6/MediaObjects/41588_2026_2732_MOESM4_ESM.xlsx

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Downloaded and opened the 718 KB supplementary workbook (20 sheets, ST1-ST19) and counted every non-empty row per sheet: the biggest usable table is ST14 with 236 gene rows spanning only 20 CNV (copy number variant) loci; ST10 has 87 gene rows over 9 loci, ST15 155 rows over 15 loci, ST12 12 rows over 4 loci. Every sheet is group-level summary statistics (odds ratios, standard errors, P values, carrier counts), not per-person records. Also downloaded and unpacked the 1.8 MB Zenodo archive (EAS_SCZ_rCNV_analysis-main.zip): it is R/Python/shell analysis scripts plus a GENCODE v19 gene annotation CSV and two small cohort description files listing 15 East Asian cohorts with their genotyping arrays (ASA, GSA, PsychArray, Omni, Human1M) and sizes (736-6,273 samples) - no CNV calls, no phenotypes. HEAD-probed six Springer supplementary slots; files 1,2,3,5,6 are PDFs (2.6 MB, 0.47 MB, 3.0 MB, 59 MB, 10 MB) and file 4 is the xlsx I opened.
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: The headline cohort size (20,903 cases, 23,258 controls), the nine East Asian genome-wide-significant loci and the 14 meta-analysis loci come from the abstract. The full Data Availability statement could not be read: the article is subscription-only (Europe PMC isOpenAccess=N, no PMCID), nature.com redirects to a login, and there is no preprint. I inferred controlled access from the cohort list (all Psychiatric Genomics Consortium / Stanley Global Asia cohorts) plus the PGC's published access policy, which requires a Memorandum of Understanding and a valid dbGaP application and hosts data on the Snellius cluster where downloading individual-level genotypes is explicitly prohibited.

a1_downloadable.note: FAIL, and this is the killer. The thing an ML project needs - per-person CNV calls with case/control status for the 44,161 individuals - is not downloadable anywhere. Every one of the 15 cohorts named in the Zenodo cohort files is a Psychiatric Genomics Consortium cohort; PGC individual-level access needs a signed Memorandum of Understanding plus an approved dbGaP application, and PGC policy states downloading individual-level genetic data from their compute cluster is strictly prohibited. What IS freely downloadable (verified by opening it) is only the group-level supplementary workbook and the analysis code.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: FAIL for every public-table project. In the public files there is no per-person disease status column at all. At the gene or locus level the 'label' is an odds ratio or P value that was itself computed from the inaccessible individual data, so it is a summary of the label, not the label.

a3_inputs_present.note: FAIL. Inputs for a person-level model (which genes each individual's deletions and duplications hit) are absent; only aggregate carrier counts per locus per cohort are published. The gene annotation CSV in the Zenodo archive is a reference file, not features for examples.

a4_units_stated.note: The one thing that is fine: the workbook labels odds ratio, standard error, P value, kilobase length thresholds and the burden metrics (KB, NSEG, NGENE, NSEG_GENIC), and the Overview sheet states all coordinates are GRCh37/hg19.

a5_enough_rows.note: FAIL, verified by counting. The largest public table (ST14) has 236 gene rows, and those collapse to 20 independent CNV loci because every gene inside one CNV shares the same statistics - e.g. DGCR8 and ARVCF both carry P = 1.19e-28 in ST15. ST5's 947 rows are the same burden test repeated across 15 cohorts x CNV type x 7 length thresholds x 4 metrics, not independent examples. Far below the ~400-row floor even for classification.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~12 MB (0.7 MB xlsx + 10 MB gene annotation CSV)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Trivially laptop-sized - but only because there is almost nothing in it.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Cohort sizes in the Zenodo cohort_annotation.txt file (736 to 6,273 per cohort, 15 cohorts) are consistent in scale with the abstract's 44,161 total; ST9a lists 14,788 cases and 15,671 controls for the polygenic-score subset, plausibly a subset. No contradiction found, though I could not read the main text to cross-check.

a8_label_provenance.note: FAIL as a consequence of A1. Any label available in public is a regression coefficient output by the authors' own PLINK/meta-analysis pipeline on data I cannot see. Predicting it from gene features such as loss-of-function intolerance would partly re-learn the paper's own finding that associated loci sit in constrained genes - leakage by construction, with no way to trace back to the underlying measurement.

existing_models.name: X-CNV (a gradient-boosting classifier that scores how damaging a copy number variant is)
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported area under the curve 0.96 training / 0.94 validation, per the search-result summary only; I did not open the paper or check the split.

existing_models.name: CNVoyant (a machine-learning classifier of clinical significance of copy number variants, trained on ~52,176 ClinVar entries)
existing_models.score_and_split: Not verified; only the search-result description was seen.

backbone.name: None applicable - no sequence, molecule or single-cell input exists in the public files; DNA language models such as Nucleotide Transformer would need per-person variant data that is not released.
backbone.licence: Zenodo code archive is CC-BY-4.0; supplementary tables carry the Nature Genetics article licence.

integration.partner_dataset: gnomAD structural variants and ClinVar copy number variants could in principle join on GRCh37 genomic coordinates, and the gene-level tables carry Ensembl gene IDs that join to GTEx or Open Targets.
integration.join_key: Ensembl gene ID (e.g. ENSG00000128191) and hg19 chromosome/start/end coordinates - both verified present in the workbook.
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: No worthwhile combined question survives, because after joining you still have only 20 loci of outcome data, which is a scatter plot, not a model.

controls.positive_control: The 22q11.21 deletion is the textbook schizophrenia copy number variant and does appear in the tables (ST15, P = 1.19e-28), so it would be an obvious positive control - but there is no model to run it against.
controls.negative_control: Label shuffling is meaningless at n = 20 loci.
controls.external_validation: European-ancestry results from Marshall et al. 2017 (Nature Genetics, 41,321 subjects) are already merged into these same tables, so they are not independent.

honest_claim_h3: With only the public files, the honest claim a model could make is: 'among 20 copy number variant loci that were already selected for study because they looked interesting in Europeans, gene annotation features correlate with effect size' - a statement about 20 data points, which is a correlation, not a model.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use each person's pattern of large DNA deletions and duplications to predict whether they have schizophrenia.
plain_idea.train_on: The project I considered would show the model, for each of the ~44,161 East Asian participants, which genes are hit by their rare deletions and duplications plus total deleted/duplicated length. That per-person table is not public; the public files contain at most 236 rows of group-level statistics covering 20 loci.
plain_idea.predict: Schizophrenia case or control status, which comes from clinical diagnosis in the original recruiting cohorts in China, Japan, Taiwan, Singapore and Indonesia.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Psychiatric genetics has been overwhelmingly European, so a model that works in East Asian populations would matter to anyone building risk scores outside Europe; but the paper itself already reports the achievable ceiling as a liability-scale R-squared of 0.0026 for copy number burden versus 0.027 for the common-variant polygenic score, so the signal is tiny even with full data.

ml_idea: Considered and rejected: a per-person classifier of schizophrenia from rare copy number variant burden and gene-hit profile, trained in East Asians and tested for transfer to Europeans. The required per-person data is behind a Psychiatric Genomics Consortium access application. The fallback - predicting locus-level effect size from gene annotation using the public tables - dies on sample size (20 independent loci) and on circularity (the label is the paper's own regression output, and the obvious feature, loss-of-function intolerance, is the paper's own finding).

effort.compute_note: Measured from the actual downloads: 718 KB supplementary workbook plus a 10 MB gene annotation CSV in the 1.8 MB Zenodo code archive. Size is irrelevant here because the content is too thin to model.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Count the independent units in the public tables. I did it: 20 unique CNV loci across 236 gene rows, with genes inside a locus sharing identical statistics. That took five minutes and kills the project.

verdict_reason: Part A1 fails: the per-person copy number variant calls and diagnoses for the 20,903 cases and 23,258 controls sit behind a Psychiatric Genomics Consortium Memorandum of Understanding plus a dbGaP application, on a cluster that forbids downloading. A5 fails independently and verifiably: everything that is public is group-level summary statistics, with the biggest table holding 236 gene rows that collapse to 20 independent CNV loci. A2 and A8 also fail, because the only available 'label' is an odds ratio the authors computed from the data I cannot see. The science is valuable - it is one of the first large non-European CNV studies of schizophrenia - but there is no ML project here without an access application.
